title: Amygdala in Trauma
subtitle: Detecting significance and learning threat
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating amygdala in trauma across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain amygdala in trauma in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in amygdala in trauma.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to amygdala in trauma.

sections.explainSimply: The amygdala helps the brain learn which cues predict danger or importance.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: It contributes to threat learning, salience, autonomic preparation and memory modulation; it is not a simple “fear centre.”
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Trauma studies often report altered amygdala reactivity and connectivity, but results vary and overlap with other conditions and normal variation.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of amygdala in trauma as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need amygdala in trauma to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: An “overactive amygdala” is a metaphor, not an individual diagnosis.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use amygdala in trauma to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses amygdala in trauma to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: An “overactive amygdala” is a metaphor, not an individual diagnosis. Evidence classification: established role; heterogeneous clinical findings.
